passage: "No! My cup!" Gargi flung the blue cup across the kitchen and wailed. "It's your favourite cup, sweetie," said her mother, Parul. "Want red!" Parul held out the red one. "No red!" Gargi dropped to the floor, kicking. "You skipped your nap at Nani's, didn't you?" Parul said, sitting down beside her. "Up," Gargi sobbed, arms stretched. "Come here. No more choices, just a cuddle in the dark room." Gargi's head sank onto her shoulder.

qa.q: Where did Gargi skip her nap?
qa.a: At Nani's.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when she refused both cups?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and frustrated; she was so tired that even choosing a cup set off screaming and kicking.

qa.q: What worked for Parul, and why?
qa.a: She stopped offering choices and took Gargi for a cuddle in the dark room, because a worn-out toddler needs rest, not more decisions.

qa.q: How does Parul see Gargi's screaming?
qa.a: Parul sees it as tiredness from the missed nap rather than naughtiness, so she stays calm and sits down beside her.

grounding: Shows a toddler who missed a nap falling apart over a tiny choice, and a parent treating it as exhaustion rather than naughtiness.

passage: Note for Himani's parents, Tuesday. Himani didn't nap today; the room was too noisy. By afternoon she was not herself. When her block tower fell, she screamed. She held on to my leg, then lay flat on the mat and cried when I offered her shoes. She wasn't being difficult; she had nothing left. I dimmed the corner lights, sat with her on the cushion and hummed. She dozed before pickup. An early night may help. Swati (room teacher)

qa.q: What happened just before Himani screamed?
qa.a: Her block tower fell.

qa.q: What might Himani have been feeling when she held on to Swati's leg?
qa.a: She was probably feeling overwhelmed and in need of comfort, because being so tired made every small upset feel too big.

qa.q: Which of Swati's steps helped, and why?
qa.a: Dimming the lights, sitting close and humming gave a worn-out toddler a calm way to rest instead of more demands.

qa.q: What might change for Himani's parents after reading the note?
qa.a: They would know the crankiness comes from the missed nap, so they could plan an early night instead of treating her as naughty.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler who skipped a nap losing all ability to cope, with small upsets turning into screaming, clinging and collapsing.

subtype: Sleepy child rubbing eyes and getting wild [Observer]
passage: At the birthday party in Leeds, two-year-old Chidi raced laps around the sofa, shrieking with laughter and rubbing his eyes. "He's full of beans!" someone said. Clara, his aunt, watched him trip over a balloon and burst into loud sobs. She scooped him up. "Not beans," she murmured. "You're done in." His eyes were red. She carried him to the quiet bedroom, drew the curtains and lay beside him. He was asleep before the second song.

qa.q: What did Chidi trip over?
qa.a: A balloon.

qa.q: What did Clara think was really going on while Chidi raced and shrieked?
qa.a: She thought he was overtired rather than just excited; the eye-rubbing and sudden sobs told her he needed sleep.

qa.q: What small step helped Chidi settle?
qa.a: Clara took him to a quiet bedroom, drew the curtains and lay beside him, giving his tired body a calm place to sleep.

qa.q: What was the party like for Chidi by the time he tripped?
qa.a: It was probably too much for him; he was so worn out that a small fall tipped his loud laughter straight into tears.

grounding: Illustrates an adult reading a toddler's wild, loud play and eye-rubbing as a sign that sleep is overdue.

subtype: Sleepy child rubbing eyes and getting wild [Observer]
passage: Most evenings I, Sharmila, sit on the bench by our building's swings. Last Thursday, little Varun from the ground floor was everywhere at once: climbing the slide the wrong way, laughing far too loudly, rubbing his eyes with both fists. "Sharmila aunty, catch me!" he yelled, then flopped onto the sand and howled when his slipper came off. His mother frowned. "Stop this drama." I said, "Maybe he's sleepy?" She looked at his droopy eyelids and carried him home.

qa.q: What did Varun do when his slipper came off?
qa.a: He flopped onto the sand and howled.

qa.q: What was Varun's mother feeling at first, and what changed her mind?
qa.a: She felt irritated and read it as drama; after Sharmila's comment, his droopy eyelids showed her he was tired.

qa.q: What small step helped here?
qa.a: Sharmila gently suggested he might be sleepy instead of joining the scolding, and his mother took him home to rest.

qa.q: How might the evening have felt for Varun?
qa.a: Probably overwhelming; his body was worn out, so he could not slow down, and a lost slipper felt huge.

grounding: Shows a neighbour noticing that a toddler's loud, wild play and eye-rubbing point to overdue sleep rather than misbehaviour.

passage: Bedtimes in Lindiwe's Cape Town flat used to be a battle: pleading, bargaining with biscuits, a sharp voice at the end. Now she runs Ivan's warm bath, switches off the big light and leaves only the lamp glowing. She sings the same short song about the moon, gives the same long cuddle and says, "Sleep now, see you in the morning." Ivan, nearly two, yawns before the song is over. He knows exactly what comes next.

qa.q: What song does Lindiwe sing?
qa.a: The same short song about the moon.

qa.q: What might Lindiwe have felt during the old bedtime battles?
qa.a: She was likely frustrated and worn out, which is why the pleading and bargaining ended in a sharp voice.

qa.q: Which change made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Swapping pleading and biscuit deals for the same bath, lamp, song and cuddle each night, because the repetition tells Ivan it is safe to sleep.

qa.q: What would change for Ivan if the routine kept shifting each night?
qa.a: He would have to guess what comes next, so bedtime would feel less safe and he would likely fuss more.

grounding: Shows a calm, repeated wind-down of bath, dim light, song and cuddle replacing scolding and bargaining at a toddler's bedtime.

passage: I stayed a week with my sister Lakshmi in Madurai and kept watching her nights with little Chinnu. Warm wash, cotton frock, tube light off, only the small lamp on. She hums the lullaby our Ammamma sang and holds him on her shoulder the same way every night. On my second evening I tried bribing him with a biscuit to lie down; he howled. Lakshmi simply began the lullaby again, and he quietened. Kavitha

qa.q: What did Kavitha try on the second evening?
qa.a: Bribing Chinnu with a biscuit to lie down.

qa.q: What does Chinnu's quietening suggest he felt when the lullaby began again?
qa.a: He felt soothed and safe, because the familiar lullaby told him what came next.

qa.q: Which approach worked better, and why?
qa.a: Lakshmi's calm return to the same lullaby worked better than the biscuit bribe, because the familiar steps settled Chinnu instead of starting a bargain.

qa.q: How does Kavitha see Lakshmi's routine by the end of the week?
qa.a: Kavitha sees that it works: the same steps every night calm Chinnu in a way a bribe could not.

grounding: Illustrates a predictable wind-down with dim light, a song and the same cuddle settling a toddler better than bargaining.

passage:
Monday: Omkar called out for water, then another story, then one more hug. His father, Nilesh, snapped, "Enough! Sleep!" Omkar cried for a long time, staring at the dark cupboard.
Wednesday: When Omkar called, Nilesh came, sat for a moment and said softly, "I'm right next door. The cupboard is just a cupboard." One sip of water, one hug.
Saturday: Omkar asked only once. "You're next door?" "Right next door." He turned over, holding his cloth rabbit.

qa.q: What did Omkar hold on Saturday?
qa.a: His cloth rabbit.

qa.q: Why did Omkar keep asking for water and hugs on Monday?
qa.a: He was scared of the dark and of being alone, so the requests were a way to keep his father close.

qa.q: What changed between Monday and Wednesday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Nilesh answered calmly and briefly instead of snapping, which reassured Omkar so he needed fewer calls.

qa.q: How does Nilesh's view of the calls seem to change over the week?
qa.a: At first he treats them as defiance and snaps; by Wednesday he answers the fear behind them with a short, calm promise.

grounding: Shows a young child stalling at bedtime out of night fear, and short calm reassurance settling it over several nights.

passage: The power went out just after bedtime, and the fan fell silent. "Appa, water!" called four-year-old Tarun. Shankar brought a steel tumbler. "Appa, one more story." "One short one." "Appa, hug?" Shankar was tired from his shift and wanted to say no. Instead he sat on the edge of the mat, his phone torch pointed at the ceiling. "The dark is the same room, kanna. I'm right here till you sleep." Tarun's fingers found his sleeve. His breathing slowed as rain began drumming on the roof.

qa.q: What did Shankar bring when Tarun asked for water?
qa.a: A steel tumbler.

qa.q: What was Tarun worried about as he kept calling out?
qa.a: He was frightened of the sudden dark and of being left alone, so he kept calling to keep his Appa close.

qa.q: What choice helped Tarun settle, and why?
qa.a: Shankar stayed calm, gave a short reassurance and sat nearby, which answered Tarun's fear instead of fighting his requests.

qa.q: What was the night like for Shankar?
qa.a: He was tired after his shift and tempted to refuse, but he chose patience over irritation.

grounding: Illustrates a young child's bedtime requests as a bid for comfort in the dark, settled by a short calm answer.

subtype: Parents worn down by broken nights [Receiver]
passage: For a week Charu had woken every night, calling for her mother after bad dreams. In their village near Moga, Gurpreet still rose before light to milk the buffalo, eyes gritty. At breakfast Charu spilled her milk, and Gurpreet shouted so loudly the dog ran off. Charu's lip shook. Later, rolling rotis, Gurpreet felt sick with guilt. "It isn't her," she told her mother-in-law. "It's me, running on no sleep." Biji took the buffalo that evening and sent Gurpreet to bed early. Next morning, Gurpreet hugged Charu first.

qa.q: What did Charu spill at breakfast?
qa.a: Her milk.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet feel while rolling rotis, and why?
qa.a: She felt guilty, because she knew she had shouted out of exhaustion, not because of anything Charu really did.

qa.q: What helped more than willpower here?
qa.a: Biji taking over the buffalo so Gurpreet could sleep early; real rest let her start the next morning gently.

qa.q: What was the shouting like for Charu?
qa.a: It frightened and hurt her; her lip shook because a small spill brought a loud, angry voice.

grounding: Shows a parent worn down by a child's repeated night waking snapping over a small thing, feeling guilty, and being helped by real rest.

subtype: Parents worn down by broken nights [Receiver]
passage: For two weeks Emil's nightmares had woken the whole Seville flat three or four times a night. On Thursday morning Emil couldn't find his left shoe. "Every single day!" Javier barked, and slammed the cupboard. Emil stood very still. On the bus, Javier replayed it and his stomach turned. That night he told his husband, Marco, "I'm not angry at Emil. I'm just empty." They agreed to take turns, and Marco handled Friday's wake-ups while Javier slept in the spare room. On Saturday, Javier knelt to tie Emil's shoes and said sorry.

qa.q: What could Emil not find on Thursday morning?
qa.a: His left shoe.

qa.q: What was Javier feeling on the bus?
qa.a: He felt guilty and upset with himself; his stomach turned as he replayed barking at Emil.

qa.q: Which plan helped, and why?
qa.a: Taking turns with the night wake-ups, so Javier finally got proper rest; sleep, not trying harder, gave him back his patience.

qa.q: How was Emil affected when Javier barked?
qa.a: Emil was startled and scared, standing very still after the cupboard slammed.

grounding: Illustrates a parent's irritation coming from their own lost sleep, the guilt afterwards, and rest rather than willpower as the fix.

passage: Raghav, ten, helped at his uncle's roadside dhaba till the last trucks pulled away, then slept on a cot beside the clattering kitchen. At the village school next morning, Masterji said, "Copy the sums from page forty, then underline the answers." Raghav copied the sums and forgot the rest. His head drooped onto his slate. "Lazy again?" Masterji asked. Raghav's eyes stung. "I'm trying, sir." His friend Kunal whispered, "You look like a ghost." At lunch Kunal let him lie in the shade of the neem tree while he kept watch, and shook him awake at the bell. That afternoon Raghav got every sum right.

qa.q: Which page did Masterji ask the class to copy sums from?
qa.a: Page forty.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling when Masterji called him lazy?
qa.a: He felt hurt and ashamed; his eyes stung because he really was trying, just too tired to keep up.

qa.q: How could Masterji support Raghav better?
qa.a: He could gently ask how Raghav is sleeping instead of calling him lazy, and talk with the family about the late nights at the dhaba.

qa.q: How does Kunal see what is happening to Raghav?
qa.a: Kunal sees a friend who is worn out rather than lazy, so he lets Raghav nap in the shade and wakes him at the bell.

grounding: Shows a sleep-deprived schoolchild forgetting instructions, getting teary and being called lazy when the real problem is a foggy, tired mind.

passage: Tariq, nine, slept on the other side of a thin wall from his new baby sister, and she cried most nights. At school in Toronto he forgot his library book, then forgot the art instructions twice. When his partner Bao took the blue paint first, Tariq shouted, "You always do that!" and then, to his own surprise, began to cry. The teacher, Ms Harper, crouched by his desk. "You look really tired. How's sleep at home?" Tariq told her about the baby. She sent a note home, and that evening his parents moved his bed into the quieter study.

qa.q: What did Bao take first?
qa.a: The blue paint.

qa.q: Why did Tariq shout at Bao and then cry?
qa.a: He was exhausted, so a small thing felt huge; then he felt surprised and overwhelmed by his own outburst.

qa.q: Which step made a real difference, and why?
qa.a: Ms Harper asking about sleep instead of scolding; it led to a note home and a quieter room, which tackled the cause rather than the behaviour.

qa.q: What might the moment have been like for Bao?
qa.a: Bao may have felt confused or hurt at being shouted at over paint, without knowing how tired Tariq was.

grounding: Illustrates a tired child forgetting instructions and becoming argumentative and teary, and an adult looking for the sleep problem behind it.

subtype: Teacher noticing yawning and short temper [Observer]
passage: Eshaan, when your Nani taught Class Four in Nagpur, the children called me Shalini Madam. There was a boy, Manoj, who always laughed first at my jokes. One winter he changed. He slumped over his desk, yawned through dictation and snapped at his bench-mate over a pencil. I nearly sent him out for not paying attention. Instead, at break, I asked him quietly how he was sleeping. He told me his family had moved into one room beside the railway line, and the night trains shook the walls. I spoke to his mother, who found him a corner away from the tracks, and I stopped marking him down for slow mornings. By spring his laugh was back.

qa.q: What shook the walls at Manoj's new home?
qa.a: The night trains.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when Manoj snapped over the pencil?
qa.a: She felt irritated enough to nearly send him out, but also puzzled, because he had always been so cheerful.

qa.q: What was the turning point in how Shalini handled Manoj, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Choosing to ask him quietly about sleep at break instead of punishing him; it uncovered the noisy trains, which a punishment would have hidden.

qa.q: What might that winter have been like for Manoj?
qa.a: He was probably worn out and cross from broken sleep, and being punished for it would have felt unfair.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a usually cheerful child turn slumped and irritable, and asking gently about sleep instead of punishing.

subtype: Teacher noticing yawning and short temper [Observer]
passage: The inspection team was due at eleven, and Raghav Sir wanted Class Three quiet and tidy. Tenzin, usually the first to wave good morning, sat slumped with his cheek on his fist, notebook unopened. When a classmate bumped his elbow, he growled, "Leave me alone!" Raghav felt the clock pressing on him; a punishment would be quicker. He crouched beside Tenzin anyway. "You seem very tired today. When did you get to bed?" Tenzin rubbed his eyes. "After tuition I had two worksheets. And my cousins were staying, so the TV was loud." Raghav let him start with the easier page and wrote in his diary for his parents: "Tenzin seems very tired. Can we talk about homework and bedtime?"

qa.q: When was the inspection team due?
qa.a: At eleven.

qa.q: Why was Raghav tempted to punish Tenzin?
qa.a: He felt pressured and anxious about the inspection, and a punishment seemed quicker than finding out what was wrong.

qa.q: What did Raghav do that helped, and what could come next?
qa.a: He asked kindly about bedtime and eased Tenzin in with an easier page; next, talking with the parents about homework and noise could fix the cause.

qa.q: How might the morning feel for Tenzin if he had been punished?
qa.a: He would likely feel misunderstood and more upset, and the real problem of late nights would stay hidden.

grounding: Illustrates a teacher under time pressure noticing a normally cheerful child's slump and temper and asking about bedtime, homework and noise.

passage:
Tuesday, well past midnight
Wide awake again. At dinner I was yawning over chemistry, but the second I lay down my brain switched on like a floodlight. Alarm goes at six for the school bus. This morning I snapped at Mummy over a missing sock, sat through first period like a zombie, and at lunch let Sumit dare me into jumping off the bike-shed roof. Landed badly on my ankle. Sumit laughed; I didn't. Mummy put ice on it, and she said we'd see the doctor if it keeps hurting or worries us. Sir says it's "attitude". Honestly, I think I'm just exhausted all the time. Tomorrow I'll ask Mummy if my phone can stay in the kitchen at night, and I'll try waking at the same time on Sunday too.
Suraj

qa.q: What did Sumit dare Suraj to do at lunch?
qa.a: Jumping off the bike-shed roof.

qa.q: How does Suraj feel about being told it is "attitude"?
qa.a: Suraj feels misunderstood and frustrated, believing the real problem is being exhausted all the time.

qa.q: Which of Suraj's plans could help, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the phone in the kitchen at night and waking at the same time on Sunday, because steady habits can ease the tiredness behind the snapping and risky dares.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the sock argument if she knew about the late nights?
qa.a: She might read the snapping as tiredness rather than rudeness and feel less hurt by it.

grounding: Shows a teenager who feels wide awake late at night but must rise early, leading to snapping, fog and a risky dare that looks like attitude.

passage:
Dolma: u awake?
Elizabeth: obviously. my brain is doing a dance party
Dolma: same. was dead sleepy at dinner, now wide awake
Elizabeth: early bus again. i'm going to be a monster tomorrow
Dolma: u WERE a monster today. u told Ms Pike her quiz was pointless
Elizabeth: i know. i felt awful after
Elizabeth: and i cycled home in the dark with no lights bc i couldn't be bothered
Dolma: Liz that's actually scary
Elizabeth: yeah. i don't even feel like me when i'm this tired
Dolma: my mum read that teen body clocks run late. not our fault but school still starts early
Elizabeth: phones out of our rooms at night and the same wake-up on weekends? deal?
Dolma: deal. and lights on ur bike tomorrow
Elizabeth: yes yes. night

qa.q: What did Elizabeth tell Ms Pike?
qa.a: That her quiz was pointless.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel after the remark to Ms Pike?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt awful afterwards and says being this tired makes it hard to feel like the usual Elizabeth.

qa.q: What small steps do Elizabeth and Dolma agree on, and why might they help?
qa.a: Phones out of their rooms at night, the same wake-up on weekends and lights on the bike, which tackle both the tiredness and the risky ride.

qa.q: How does Dolma react to the ride with no lights?
qa.a: Dolma finds it genuinely scary and sees it as a risky choice that comes from being worn out, not from not caring.

grounding: Illustrates teenagers whose bodies feel alert late at night while school starts early, leading to low mood, sharp remarks and a risky choice.

subtype: Parent fighting with a sleepy teen [Receiver]
passage:
Monday, at dawn: "Tushar! Third time! Up!" Rajni pounded on his door. A grunt. Then the bathroom door slammed, and mother and son left the house without a kind word.
Thursday evening: Rajni sat on the end of his bed. "I'm tired of fighting. I read that teenagers' bodies want to sleep later. What would help?" Tushar blinked, surprised. They agreed his phone would charge in the hall at night, and he would wake to his own alarm at the same time every day, weekends included.
The next Monday: his alarm rang once. Tushar shuffled into the kitchen, hair wild, and muttered, "Morning." Rajni passed him his tea. No doors slammed.

qa.q: Where does Tushar's phone charge at night after the deal?
qa.a: In the hall.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling on the first Monday when he slammed the door?
qa.a: He felt angry and cornered; being shouted awake while groggy made him defensive.

qa.q: What changed on Thursday, and why did it work better than shouting?
qa.a: Rajni talked calmly and asked what would help, and they agreed on a phone rule and a steady wake time; Tushar had a say, so he kept to it.

qa.q: How were the early mornings affecting Rajni at first?
qa.a: She was frustrated and worn down, calling three times and starting her own day angry.

grounding: Shows a parent's dawn shouting drawing grunts and slammed doors, and a calm talk about teen sleep leading to agreed phone and wake-up rules.

subtype: Parent fighting with a sleepy teen [Receiver]
passage: Rashmi, you shout at your son Aman every morning the way I, Rajni, once shouted at your brother Deepak. I'd stand at his door at dawn: "Up! Up! Are you a buffalo?" He'd grunt, the door would slam twice, and neither of us said a kind word before school. One day his teacher told me many teenagers simply can't fall asleep early; their bodies run later. I thought it was an excuse. Still, one Sunday I stopped yelling and sat down with Deepak. We agreed the radio went off after dinner and he'd wake at the same time every day, even holidays, with his own clock. He grumbled, but the slamming stopped. We started talking again at breakfast.

qa.q: What did Rajni used to shout at Deepak's door?
qa.a: "Up! Up! Are you a buffalo?"

qa.q: What did Rajni feel when the teacher explained teen sleep?
qa.a: She felt doubtful, even dismissive, thinking it was just an excuse.

qa.q: What was the turning point with Deepak, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Rajni stopped yelling and sat down with him to agree on the radio going off after dinner and a steady wake time; he had a say, so the slamming stopped.

qa.q: How might those dawn shouts have felt to Deepak?
qa.a: Harsh and humiliating when he was already groggy, which is why he answered with grunts and slammed doors.

grounding: Illustrates a parent learning that shouting at a sleepy teen breeds slammed doors, while understanding and a negotiated routine repair the relationship.

passage: Chaitanya, you want to stay up all night before physics? Let your Pradeep Chacha tell you about Class Twelve. I drank strong coffee and sat up with my notes till the birds started. I believed every hour awake was another chapter learnt. In the exam hall my hands shook, and I read a question on lenses three times without understanding it. Formulas I knew by heart had simply gone. I panicked and wrote half answers. Before the next paper, my friend Latha sat me down, and she made me a plan: hard chapters in the afternoon, a light look in the evening, and bed at the usual time. I walked in calm and remembered far more. The sleep was part of the studying.

qa.q: Which question did Pradeep read three times?
qa.a: A question on lenses.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling in the exam hall?
qa.a: He felt panicked and shaken; his hands shook and formulas he knew by heart had gone.

qa.q: What was the turning point before the next paper, and why did it help?
qa.a: Following Latha's plan to study the hard chapters earlier and go to bed at the usual time; rested, he walked in calm and remembered more.

qa.q: How might Latha have seen Pradeep's all-night habit?
qa.a: Latha probably saw it was hurting more than helping, which is why the plan kept his sleep.

grounding: Shows a student who crams all night believing more hours awake mean more learning, then panics and forgets, and a calmer plan that protects sleep.

passage: The night before the chemistry exam, a wedding band thundered two lanes away, and Varun gave up on sleep. "I'll just go through everything once more," he told himself, and when the power went too, he kept cramming by torchlight. By dawn the equations swam. On the way to the bus he couldn't recall the first flashcard, and his chest felt tight. His sister Indu stopped walking. "Breathe with me. In. Out. You've studied for weeks. You're not starting from zero." He breathed slowly and wrote what he could. That evening Indu helped him plan for the next paper: finish revising by dinner, then earplugs and lights out.

qa.q: What was thundering the night before the chemistry exam?
qa.a: A wedding band, two lanes away.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling on the way to the bus?
qa.a: He felt panicky; his chest was tight and he could not recall the first flashcard.

qa.q: What is wiser about the plan for the next paper?
qa.a: Finishing revision by dinner and then sleeping means he goes in rested instead of foggy and panicked.

qa.q: How does Indu see Varun's panic?
qa.a: She sees him as prepared but exhausted, so she calms his breathing and reminds him he has studied for weeks.

grounding: Illustrates a student cramming through the night, facing foggy memory and rising panic the next day, then planning to protect sleep before the next exam.
